title: Walking pilgrimage
hook: the Camino to Santiago, Lourdes, Jerusalem: walking as prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Divine Office: prayer by the clock, day and night. Your line was the hours.

Tied to the back of a dusty backpack, a scallop shell bounces with every step. The person wearing it has blisters, a walking stick, and a little booklet that gets stamped in towns along the way. Ahead are more days of the same: up early, walk, eat, sleep in a bunk room full of strangers, walk again. The road is the Camino, the Way of Saint James, and it ends at a cathedral in Santiago, in the northwest corner of Spain. Ask walkers why they're doing it, and the answers run all over the place. Grief. Faith. A birthday. A divorce. No idea yet.
screen: `A SCALLOP SHELL ON A BACKPACK.` → `A BOOKLET STAMPED ALONG THE WAY.` → `GRIEF, FAITH, NO IDEA YET.`

segments.voice: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place, made as an act of devotion. Christians walk to many such places; here are three, and the thread that runs through them. First, Santiago. Tradition says the apostle James is buried there, and pilgrims walk to his tomb, some wearing the scallop shell as their sign. Second, Lourdes, in the south of France. Catholic tradition holds that Mary appeared there to a young girl named Bernadette, beside a grotto with a spring. Pilgrims come to pray, to bathe in the water, and to bring the sick. Third, Jerusalem. Christian pilgrims walk the Via Dolorosa, the way of sorrows, stopping to pray at stations along the route Jesus is remembered to have carried his cross. And the thread runs back into the Bible. Its Book of Psalms has a group of songs headed "A Song of degrees," which some readers take as songs for going up to Jerusalem. One of them begins: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." And then: "Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem." Our feet. Not our thoughts. On a pilgrimage the body does the praying: the distance, the weather, the ache in the legs, the strangers who share bread. Some walkers say the arrival matters less than they expected, and the road matters more. Prayer doesn't have to sit still. Here it gets up and walks.
screen: `SANTIAGO: THE SCALLOP SHELL.` · `LOURDES: THE GROTTO AND THE SPRING.` · `JERUSALEM: THE WAY OF SORROWS.` · `OUR FEET SHALL STAND.` · then, large: `I WAS GLAD WHEN THEY SAID UNTO ME.`

segments.voice: Choose a destination close by, a window, a doorway, a plant, a tree outside, and before you set off, name one thing you're carrying: a hope, a worry, a person. Walk to it slowly, the way you'd walk the last stretch to a cathedral, feeling each foot land. When you arrive, stay there; if you pray, offer what you carried, and if not, just let yourself arrive.
Walking pilgrimage. A journey on foot to a holy place, Santiago, Lourdes, Jerusalem, where the walking itself becomes the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: walking as prayer. Our feet shall stand within thy gates. See you tomorrow.
